lead: In Scripture, pride and humility are not merely differences in personality. They concern where a person places himself before God. This study brings together the plumb line of Amos, the Hebrew and Greek terms for pride and humility, poverty of spirit, self-humbling, purity, and the obedience of Yeshua, who humbled Himself unto death.

blocks.text: Scripture quotations are based on the King James Version (KJV), with ‘Jesus’ rendered as ‘Yeshua’ and the divine name rendered as ‘YHWH’ where appropriate.

In Scripture, pride and humility are not merely differences in personality. They concern where a person places himself before God. When we read only the translated terms, words such as pride, arrogance, haughtiness, self-exaltation, humility, lowliness, and abasement can appear to mean almost the same thing. In Hebrew and Greek, however, these words often carry different emphases. Understanding these distinctions helps us see more clearly why God warns against a heart that exalts itself and gives grace to those who are poor in spirit and humble themselves before Him.
Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall. Better it is to be of an humble spirit with the lowly, than to divide the spoil with the proud.

One of the important Hebrew words associated with ‘pride’ in Proverbs 16:18 is גָּאוֹן (ga'on). It can mean height, majesty, exaltation, or pride. When used of God, it may describe His majesty and excellence. When used of human beings who exalt themselves, however, it carries the meaning of pride. The expression גֹּבַהּ רוּחַ (govah ruach) in the latter part of the verse literally refers to a ‘high spirit’ or an ‘exalted spirit.’ At the root of biblical pride, therefore, lies the elevation of oneself and the tendency to treat one’s own judgment, ability, or position as supreme.
Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful.

The word underlying the ‘scornful’ in Psalm 1:1 is לֵץ (lets), with the plural לֵצִים (letsim). Its central meaning is not simply someone who thinks highly of himself. It refers to a mocker, scoffer, or one who treats correction with contempt. Thus, this form of arrogance goes beyond self-exaltation. It includes the attitude of making light of wisdom, rebuke, and even the word of God. In Proverbs, לֵץ (lets) repeatedly describes a person who resists correction and refuses instruction.

Other Hebrew words related to arrogance and haughtiness include זֵד (zed) and יָהִיר (yahir). זֵד (zed) can describe someone who is presumptuous, insolent, or willfully exceeds his proper place. יָהִיר (yahir) carries the sense of being haughty or arrogantly self-exalting. When inward self-exaltation becomes outward speech and conduct that despise others and reject instruction, arrogance has moved from an inward disposition into a visible way of life.

What we call ‘self-conceit’ or ‘self-exaltation’ is not always represented by one specific Hebrew word. Scripture frequently describes it as the heart becoming lifted up. In Deuteronomy 8:14, the expression וְרָם לְבָבֶךָ (ve-ram levavekha) means that ‘thine heart be lifted up.’ Verse 17 then describes the accompanying thought that one’s own power and strength have produced one’s prosperity. Biblical self-exaltation is therefore closely connected with attributing one’s wisdom, ability, success, and possessions ultimately to oneself.
Then thine heart be lifted up, and thou forget YHWH thy God … And thou say in thine heart, My power and the might of mine hand hath gotten me this wealth.

On the opposite side stands the important Hebrew word עָנָו (anav). It describes one who is humble, meek, or lowly. This is the word used of Moses in Numbers 12:3 when he is described as very meek. Biblical humility is not the denial of one’s worth or a form of self-hatred. It is the accurate recognition of one’s position before God and the refusal to exalt oneself.

A related Hebrew word is עָנִי (ani), which may mean poor, afflicted, needy, or brought low. Depending on the context, it may refer to material poverty, but it can also describe a condition in which a person recognizes that he cannot deliver himself by his own strength and must depend upon God. For this reason, poverty and lowliness in the Hebrew Scriptures are often connected with dependence upon God.

Another important expression is שְׁפַל־רוּחַ (shefal-ruach), meaning one who is ‘lowly in spirit.’ The adjective שָׁפָל (shafal) means low or brought low. Isaiah 57:15 speaks of God dwelling with דַּכָּא וּשְׁפַל־רוּחַ (dakka u-shefal-ruach), the contrite and humble in spirit. דַּכָּא (dakka) carries the sense of being crushed, broken, or contrite. This does not mean destroying one’s sense of human worth. It means that self-righteousness and self-exaltation have been broken so that the person acknowledges that he cannot stand before God apart from His mercy.

A representative Hebrew verb associated with humbling oneself is כָּנַע (kana). In 2 Chronicles 7:14, God calls His people to humble themselves, pray, seek His face, and turn from their wicked ways. The verb has a semantic range that includes being brought low, subdued, subjected, or humbled. In a reflexive sense, it expresses the act of humbling oneself. Biblical humility, therefore, is not merely speaking politely or appearing modest. It involves laying down self-rule and self-righteousness and submitting oneself before God.

If my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then will I hear from heaven, and will forgive their sin, and will heal their land.

Micah 6:8 uses the expression הַצְנֵעַ לֶכֶת (hatsnea lekhet) in speaking of walking humbly with God. The idea is not that of walking through life in self-display or self-promotion, but of walking carefully, modestly, and humbly with God. Biblical humility is therefore not only an inward attitude. It becomes a way of life.

In the New Testament, Yeshua speaks of those who are ‘poor in spirit.’ The Greek expression in Matthew 5:3 is πτωχοὶ τῷ πνεύματι (ptōchoi tō pneumati). The adjective πτωχός (ptōchos) means poor, destitute, needy, or dependent upon help. To be poor in spirit therefore does not mean lacking confidence or possessing a passive personality. It means recognizing one’s spiritual poverty before God and one’s complete need for His mercy and grace.
Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.

This is the opposite of self-righteousness. A person who regards himself as righteous and presents his own merit before God stands very differently from a person who recognizes his sin and insufficiency and asks for God’s mercy. Biblical humility does not falsely declare oneself worthless. It acknowledges one’s true condition before God and seeks grace.

The same principle appears when Yeshua describes Himself. In Matthew 11:29, πραΰς (praus) means meek or gentle, while ταπεινὸς τῇ καρδίᾳ (tapeinos tē kardia) means ‘lowly in heart.’ The adjective ταπεινός (tapeinos) means low, humble, or lowly. The humility of Yeshua was not an abstract quality. It was revealed in the concrete way He lived and submitted Himself.
Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls.

The verb ταπεινόω (tapeinoō) in Philippians 2:8 means to humble or lower. The expression ἐταπείνωσεν ἑαυτόν (etapeinōsen heauton) literally means that ‘He humbled Himself.’ God, having come in human flesh, lived fully within the human condition and followed the will of the Father to the end, becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.

Let this mind be in you, which was also in Messiah Yeshua: Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God: But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men: And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him.

Scripture also requires us to distinguish between being brought low and possessing humility. A lowly condition may refer simply to one’s outward circumstances, whereas humility includes the inward disposition and conduct of refusing to exalt oneself and submitting to God even in that condition. When Paul says in Philippians 4:12 that he knows how to be abased, the emphasis is on knowing how to live in lowly circumstances. A person is not automatically humble because he is poor or socially low, nor is a person automatically proud because he occupies a high position. The decisive issue is where the heart stands before God.

Scripture also connects humility with purity. The Hebrew expression נְקִי כַפַּיִם (neqi kappayim) in Psalm 24 describes one who has ‘clean hands.’ The hands represent conduct and actions. The expression לֵב טָהוֹר (lev tahor) in Psalm 51 means a ‘clean’ or ‘pure heart.’ In the New Testament, the ‘pure in heart’ are described as καθαροὶ τῇ καρδίᾳ (katharoi tē kardia), and καθαρός (katharos) means clean, pure, or undefiled. James 4 likewise places drawing near to God, cleansing the hands, purifying the heart, and humbling oneself before the Lord within one connected movement.

God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble … Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you. Cleanse your hands, ye sinners; and purify your hearts, ye double minded … Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he shall lift you up.

When these biblical terms are considered together, the structure of pride and humility becomes clearer. The heart can become lifted up and begin to rely upon its own power. This may develop into self-exaltation and pride, and from there into arrogance that looks down upon others. If it progresses further until a person despises correction and mocks the word of God, he begins to display the character of לֵץ (lets), the scoffer.

The opposite movement is also clear. Poverty of spirit recognizes one’s need and insufficiency before God. Humility refuses to exalt oneself. Humbling oneself involves laying down self-righteousness and self-rule before God. Purity of heart and clean hands show that this inward posture must also become visible in life.
Against this background, the vision of the plumb line in Amos 7 becomes especially significant.

The Hebrew word in Amos 7:7–8 is אֲנָךְ ('anakh). It has traditionally been understood as referring to a plumb line or plummet. It is, however, a rare Hebrew word whose precise etymology is uncertain. Scholarly discussion has therefore continued concerning its exact meaning. Some interpretations connect it with an ancient Semitic term for a metal, possibly lead or tin, and understand it as referring to the material of a plumb weight. Thus, while the traditional interpretation of a ‘plumb line’ remains widely used and provides a coherent reading of the passage, the precise lexical meaning of the term remains a matter of scholarly discussion.

Thus he shewed me: and, behold, YHWH stood upon a wall made by a plumbline, with a plumbline in his hand. And YHWH said unto me, Amos, what seest thou? And I said, A plumbline. Then said YHWH, Behold, I will set a plumbline in the midst of my people Israel: I will not again pass by them any more: And the high places of Isaac shall be desolate, and the sanctuaries of Israel shall be laid waste; and I will rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword.

Under the traditional plumb-line interpretation, the plumb line is not primarily a destructive instrument like a sword or hammer. Its first function is measurement. It reveals what is straight and what is out of alignment. Yet in Amos 7 the act of measurement is immediately followed by the declaration that God will no longer pass by Israel and by the announcement of coming judgment. The entire vision therefore belongs unmistakably to a context of judgment. The plumb line functions as the standard by which divine judgment is rendered.

When a plumb line is lowered straight beside a wall, the line becomes the point of reference. If the wall departs from that line, the problem does not lie with the plumb line. The wall itself is out of alignment. In the same way, before the standard of God, the decisive question is not whether a person declares himself righteous according to his own measure. The question is whether his condition is aligned with the righteousness and holiness of God.

The text of Amos itself does not explicitly say that the plumb line is God Himself or that it represents the Messiah who was to come. Biblical interpretation and theological application should therefore be distinguished. Nevertheless, if the plumb line represents the standard by which God examines His people, the image can be extended theologically in the light of the New Testament. In Yeshua, God who came in human flesh, the will, righteousness, and character of God were revealed among humanity in their fullness. In this sense, Yeshua enables us to see concretely the divine standard before which human beings stand.

Before that standard, outward appearance is not enough. Yeshua compared certain religious leaders of His day to whited sepulchres. They could appear clean and righteous outwardly while being inwardly filled with uncleanness, hypocrisy, and iniquity. External religious form cannot make a person righteous when the inner person remains filled with greed, self-righteousness, and pride.
Pride, arrogance, haughtiness, and self-exaltation are different manifestations of a heart that has raised itself before God.

By contrast, one who is poor in spirit does not attempt to stand before God on the basis of his own righteousness. He acknowledges his insufficiency and seeks God’s mercy and compassion. One who mourns does not treat sin lightly. One who is pure in heart does not seek only to appear clean outwardly but desires that the inner person also be pure before God. One who is meek and humble does not use strength or position to crush others.
The most complete manifestation of this humility is found in Yeshua.

God came in human flesh, yet within the human condition Yeshua did not exalt Himself. He humbled Himself and obeyed the Father unto death. The cross was the deepest point of that self-humbling. Yeshua did not turn away from public humiliation, shame, suffering, or death. As Hebrews testifies, He endured the cross and despised the shame. His humility did not mean denying who He was. Rather, having come in human flesh, He fully embraced the path of human obedience and fulfilled the will of the Father.
Looking unto Yeshua the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God.

The meaning of His obedience is therefore greater than simply enduring suffering. God who came in human flesh personally walked the path of righteousness and obedience required of humanity. He did not merely command others to obey. He entered human existence and Himself passed through the path of obedience.
He humbled Himself unto death and gave His life as a ransom. He passed through suffering, shame, and death and was raised from the dead.

Philippians 2 places exaltation immediately after this humiliation. Because Yeshua humbled Himself and became obedient unto death, God highly exalted Him. The biblical pattern is therefore not that one exalts oneself in order to become great. Rather, the one who humbles himself before God is exalted by God.
Yeshua Himself walked this path.

God who came in human flesh fulfilled, within the human condition, the righteousness and obedience that God required. After His resurrection, Yeshua was highly exalted and seated at the right hand of God. His enemies are to be placed beneath His feet, and all things are ultimately brought under His rule.

First Corinthians 15 then describes the consummation of this order: when all things have been subjected to Messiah, the Son Himself is also subject to the One who subjected all things to Him, so that God may be all in all.

Thus, the humility and obedience of Yeshua belong to the whole work of salvation. Yeshua is the head of those who believe, and those who belong to Him become the people and temple of God. What God began by coming among humanity is carried through the death, resurrection, reign, and final restoration accomplished through Yeshua.
For the believer, therefore, the question of pride and humility is not merely a matter of personality or etiquette. It concerns how we understand our place before God.

Human beings possess a powerful desire to exalt themselves. Even feelings of inferiority can sometimes be transformed into an intense desire to prove one’s worth or superiority. A healthy sense of dignity or confidence is not itself sinful. Yet when it becomes detached from God and turns into a means of absolutizing oneself or elevating oneself above others, it can become pride.

Biblical humility does not require a person to deny every gift or ability he possesses. If a person has ability, he does not have to pretend that he has none. Rather, he recognizes the ultimate source of that ability and refuses to use it as a reason for self-exaltation.

When something is accomplished, the humble person does not say in his heart that it was achieved solely by his own wisdom and power. He acknowledges the grace, opportunity, strength, and gifts that God has given.
A humble person therefore does not deny his abilities. He simply refuses to make those abilities the foundation of self-glory.
He may have accomplishments, but he does not use them to despise others.
When he is corrected, he does not reject truth merely in order to protect his pride.
When his error is exposed, he can acknowledge it and humble himself again before God.
This is the posture of one who is poor in spirit.
The proud person believes that he is sufficient in himself. The one who is poor in spirit knows that he continually needs the grace of God.
The self-exalting person relies upon his own strength. The humble person relies upon God.
The haughty person lowers others in order to elevate himself. The one who humbles himself lowers himself before God.
The scoffer despises correction. The one who is poor in spirit examines himself before the word of God.
For this reason, the plumb line of Amos must first be applied to ourselves before we use it to measure others.
It is easy to hold the standard of God beside another person and point out where that person is out of alignment. Scripture, however, calls us first to place our own hearts before that standard.
Has my heart become lifted up?
Do I believe that what I have achieved was accomplished by my own strength alone?
Do I secretly despise others?
Do I dismiss the parts of God’s word or correction that I do not want to hear?
Do I appear clean outwardly while greed, self-righteousness, rivalry, or pride has accumulated within?
At the same time, we must look to Yeshua.
The One who is exalted above all humbled Himself.
He did not take the path of self-exaltation but took the form of a servant.
He entered the human condition and obeyed.
He humbled Himself unto death, and God highly exalted Him.

The path of the believer therefore is not the path of raising oneself but of following Yeshua and humbling oneself before God. It is the path of seeking mercy rather than boasting in one’s own righteousness, acknowledging grace rather than boasting in one’s own strength, and faithfully serving in the place God has given rather than striving to stand above others.
The many biblical terms concerning pride and humility ultimately point in one direction.

We are to turn away from the heart that exalts itself, recognize our true position before God, cleanse our hands and purify our hearts, lay down self-righteousness, remain poor in spirit, and seek the grace of God.
God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble.

When we daily take upon ourselves the mind of Yeshua, humble ourselves, give glory to God for what has been accomplished, and confess that it was not by our wisdom and ability alone, we remain within the grace of God.
And when we continually examine our hearts before the divine plumb line, that standard ceases to be merely a measure by which we judge others.
It becomes first the standard by which God brings our own lives into alignment.
